title: When the AI makes every feature cheap, how do you stop adding features?
author: shanebrumback
selftext:
Something I didn't expect from building a browser game with AI agents: the hard part stopped being "can I build this" and became "should I".

When a new pickup type, a gunship, or a whole game mode takes an afternoon instead of a month, it's very tempting to say yes to all of it. But every feature still costs something later. More to balance, more to test, more for the agent to keep in its head, more ways for an old system to break.

I'm in the middle of this with my own game, adding team multiplayer, and I've caught myself adding things because they were easy, not because players asked.

Questions for anyone shipping with AI help:

1. Do you keep a written scope or "not doing" list that the agent also reads, so it pushes back on extras?
2. How do you decide a feature earned its place? Playtests, analytics, gut feel?
3. Have you ever cut a feature the AI built quickly? Was it hard to let go of, since it was "free"?
4. Does fast building change how you plan at all, or do you still plan like it's the old cost?

Curious whether people are seeing the same thing, or if I'm just bad at saying no.

(For context, I write about AI game-dev workflows on my own site, shanebrumback.com.)
